title: Acetylide: NaNH₂ deprotonates propyne, then SN2 on CH₃Br
intent: After this scene the learner can say: "A terminal alkyne C–H has pKa 25. NH₃ has pKa 36, so NH₂⁻ is strong enough to pull that H off (equilibrium favours the weaker acid); HO⁻ is not. The acetylide carbon now has a lone pair and attacks CH₃Br from the back side in one step, pushing Br⁻ out: a new C–C bond and a longer chain. Only methyl or primary halides work."

beats.caption: Propyne and NaNH₂. The H on the end carbon of a triple bond is weakly acidic: pKa about 25.
NH₃ (pKa 36) is a weaker acid than propyne (25). Equilibrium favours the weaker acid, so NH₂⁻ wins.
beats.notes: Show a small pKa ruler (15.7 water, 25 alkyne, 36 NH₃) along the bottom edge; highlight 25 → 36 as "downhill".

beats.caption: A lone pair on N takes the H⁺. The C–H pair stays on C1 as a lone pair: the acetylide anion.

arrows.why: A lone pair on the amide N (a strong base) takes the terminal H as H⁺ and forms a new N–H bond.
The C–H bond pair stays on carbon as a lone pair. The carbon is now C⁻: the acetylide anion.

beats.caption: The acetylide carbon has a lone pair and a − charge. It is a strong nucleophile as well as a base.
beats.captionOrbitals: The pair sits in an sp orbital (50% s), held close to C. That is why this C–H was acidic.

beats.caption: CH₃Br arrives. Its C is δ+, and the side of that C facing away from Br is open: the back side.
One step: the acetylide pair bonds to C from the back as the C–Br pair leaves with Br. CH₃ flips inside out.

arrows.why: The acetylide lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon from the back and forms a new C–C bond. The chain gets longer.
The C–Br pair leaves with Br, which becomes Br⁻. That keeps the carbon at four bonds.

beats.notes: Umbrella flip: the three H of atom 6 swing from pointing at the acetylide to pointing away (Walden inversion), timed to the dots. No stereo consequence on CH₃.

beats.caption: But-2-yne. A new C–C bond formed, so the chain grew from three carbons to four.
This works only on methyl or primary halides. On a crowded carbon the back side is blocked.

stereoCallout.title: Back side, inversion
stereoCallout.text: SN2 is one step with attack opposite the leaving group, so the carbon is inverted (umbrella flip). On CH₃Br this has no visible result; on a chiral 2° carbon it would invert R/S, but acetylides do not use 2° halides (crowded back side). Chapter 7 studies SN2 itself.

quiz.q: Why is NaNH₂, not NaOH, used to make the acetylide from propyne?

options.text: NH₃ (pKa 36) is a weaker acid than the alkyne (25), so NH₂⁻ can take the H; H₂O (15.7) is stronger, so HO⁻ cannot.
options.why: Yes. An acid–base equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid.

options.text: NaOH would add OH across the triple bond.
options.why: HO⁻ does not add to the alkyne here. The only issue is acid strength: HO⁻ is too weak a base.

options.text: NH₂⁻ is smaller, so it reaches the H more easily.
options.why: Size is not it. Compare pKa values: the base works only if its conjugate acid is weaker than the alkyne.

notes: Lesson 12 s15 uses acetylene + CH₃Br (draws SN2 as "just the electron flow"); the hub example is propyne + CH₃CH₂Br → pent-2-yne. The scene uses the hub substrate with the brief's CH₃Br (→ but-2-yne, which feeds scene 10).
σ* is one step beyond the course; it lives only in the ORBITALS layer.
